messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Vignette:
Tavita is a 51-year-old married American man of Oceanian background who has spent most of his adult life working as a welder. He describes himself as someone who was used to hard physical work, long shifts, noise, heat, and the ordinary risks of a shop floor. The event he keeps returning to happened while he was driving home after work. Another car struck his vehicle with enough force that he was trapped in the seat, twisted and pinned in a way his body still seems to remember better than his mind can control. What has stayed with him is not a single picture but the whole collision arriving at once: the violent impact, the angle of his torso jammed against the seat belt and door, the noise of traffic around him, and the smell in the other car when people came near enough for him to notice it. He recalls registering alcohol on someone’s breath or clothes at the scene, and that detail remains especially potent to him now, as if that smell carries the entire crash inside it.

In the weeks after the collision, Tavita noticed that certain moments did not feel like remembering at all. If he passed a roadside accident and saw damaged cars, even briefly, he did not experience it as a distant reminder. He felt himself pulled back into the wreck with such force that his whole body seemed to assume the same position it had been in when he was trapped. He would stiffen, lean, and brace without meaning to, as though he were once again folded into metal and unable to move freely. When this happened, he also felt pain in the same parts of his body that had hurt during the crash. He spoke about this with a kind of frustrated certainty: it was not just that he thought about the pain; he felt it, sharply and specifically, in the same places.

The same thing happens with sound. Ordinary car noises can abruptly overtake him—the screech or thud of traffic outside, engines passing too close, the layered sound of vehicles in a busy roadway. At work, where the shop opens onto a road and cars can be heard intermittently through the day, he finds himself going tense before he can think through why. On some days a sound from outside is enough to stop him mid-task. For a moment the welding bay is gone and the crash feels completely real across all his senses at once. He is back in the vehicle, his body set in that trapped posture, pain flaring where he was injured, hearing traffic as danger rather than background noise. Because his trade requires steadiness and concentration, these episodes have become especially disruptive. He has begun stepping away from the noisier side of the workshop when he can, lingering longer on indoor tasks, and taking routes to work that reduce the chances of passing fresh accidents on the road.

The smell of alcohol is another powerful jolt. In everyday life it catches him off guard in ways he never anticipated: on a customer who comes into the shop after lunch, on someone standing too close at a gas station, even faintly on a passerby. He does not describe this as simple dislike. What frightens him is how instantly the smell seems to collapse time. The crash is not something that happened then; it is happening again, with the same sensory force and the same pain. He has become watchful in public for cues he associates with the collision, scanning other drivers, noticing damaged vehicles, reacting to traffic noise before his wife is even aware of it. He has not built an elaborate explanation for these reactions so much as a practical one: certain things are dangerous because they make the crash come back in full.

Over the months this has narrowed his world. His wife has noticed that he is more particular about where he will drive and more uneasy in traffic-heavy areas. At work he still shows up, but the effort it takes to stay composed around road noise leaves him tired and irritable by the end of the day. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent moment when he saw two cars pulled over after a collision on his commute. He managed to keep driving, but once he reached the shop he had to sit down because his body had locked into that old position and the pain came rushing back so convincingly that he was afraid something had physically happened to him again. He is coming for treatment because he wants his life to feel like the present rather than a series of sudden returns to the crash. What he fears most is that these moments will keep ambushing him at work, on the road, and in front of his wife, and that he will never again be able to trust his own body when memory takes hold.
